items.title: The final verdict on Formula E's Gen3 era
items.author: Sam Smith
items.content:
Formula E will begin its fourth era of technical regulations later this year and it will be a huge step up in power that will affect the sporting landscape significantly until 2030 at least.

How it got there is largely through the car that went before it, the Gen3, and since 2025, the Gen3 Evo. For good and bad, that car has informed Formula E's growth a great deal as the championship reaches a level of pace and power that will likely grab more and more fans' and investors' attention.

Born during the Covid-19 pandemic era, as a project Gen3 was a massive challenge for the FIA and Formula E Operations. That was one that was largely met, but along the way there were myriad difficulties and flashpoints.

"Welcome to the farce." That was how one team principal greeted this writer walking through the paddock gates at Valencia in early December 2022.

The Race had heard about the issues and accidents in private testing of the Gen3 car. Theo Pourchaire had ended up atop a sandbank at Calafat; Sam Bird, in a Jaguar-run car, had escaped a scary-sounding shunt at the same track; Oliver Rowland had bruised his legs in a crash at Mallory Park; and Mahindra's Lucas di Grassi severely damaged his car at Almeria. There were others too that were not quite as damaging.

Why these accidents were happening was essentially because there were no rear traction brakes on the Gen3 cars. Through the design of the Gen3 it was deemed that regen and brake-by-wire systems would be enough. They weren't.

If the powertrains hit issues and shut down, which they frequently did, drivers were left with zero braking capability as they headed for a wall (or, in the case of Pourchaire, a sandbank protecting a field).

That salty paddock greeting from the team principal was still a shock though, because it was said with such disdain and resignation. At this point Formula E was in a real crisis, no doubt about it.

Teams were unsure about the safety of their cars; drivers were actively worried and some manufacturers were even looking at their insurance and human resource compliance policies to see if they could legally compete knowing of the issues.

All the while the opening race in Mexico City was just a few weeks away and there was no chance whatsoever of getting emergency braking systems fitted to the cars before they left Europe. Things were getting fraught. And then Sebastien Buemi wrote off his Envision-Jaguar in the Valencia test. This time it was public and all hell broke loose.

Suddenly, there was open talk of the season opener being postponed. Meetings took place almost every hour at Valencia. A solution had to be found.

Eventually it was with a secondary, solenoid-activated braking system applied for the second event in Saudi Arabia. It went some way to appeasing the teams and drivers. For Mexico City, extra Tecpro barriers were fitted to some corners. Despite this, Mitch Evans had a big shunt and for several hours Jaguar and Envision considered withdrawing. They were talked down.

There were several other issues too. A shortage of spares was one other major obstacle to overcome. The fact that around nine cars were destroyed or significantly damaged (Max Guenther's Maserati at Diriyah; Edoardo Mortara (Maserati) and Pascal Wehrlein (Porsche) at Cape Town; and a quarter of the grid at Rome!) did little to help matters, but such was the conflation of the Gen3 cars with some gnarly tracks such as Rome and Diriyah that this level of chaos felt almost inevitable in the first season of the era.

Just for extra pain, the teams and manufacturers were now working under a cost cap of €13million and €15m respectively across two seasons.

When Mortara piled into Bird in Formula E's most cataclysmic ever accident in Rome, you could see the colour draining from his Maserari team principal James Rossiter's cheeks in real time. In a way that vision kind of encapsulated a wild west-like first Gen3 season.

"It was challenging but I think in the long-term memory of Formula E, Gen3 will be seen as a key step of the championship in terms of achieving a huge technological leap in efficiency."

That is the verdict of FIA championship manager for Formula E, Pablo Martino, who tells The Race he believes the recovery from that 2022 and 2023 period was successfully pulled off.

He's probably right, because by 2024 Formula E had more stability in all corners of the paddock. The Gen3 project had solidified, the racing was generally very good, and Formula E had a new, dynamic and engaging CEO in Jeff Dodds, who replaced Jamie Reigle in June 2023.

By the second season, the racing itself had developed past the initial inability of the cars to lay down the extra 50kW of attack mode power, largely because the spec tyres, supplied by Hankook, were so hard.

This led to a new form of racing, peloton or pack racing. As drivers managed useable energy knowing that the attack mode would lose them track position, a weird type of high-speed queuing pursuit took effect.

Races would then explode into life, and often carbonfibre shards too, when the pace quickened in relation to the energy targets being hit. Then the pace was unleashed and the action got really fraught, often resulting in cars running three or four abreast. It sometimes resembled a trippy kind of single-seater Talladega NASCAR scene.

At some tracks it worked fine but at wide-open expanses such as Portland, Berlin and Misano, it became essentially a tactical contact sport with front wings (brittle on the original Gen3 car) scattered around the place like confetti.

"Yes, we had maybe chaotic races, but it was also one of the most exciting periods in terms of unpredictability on track and multiple winners or multiple champion possibilities," appraises Martino now.

"I think the playing field across the different teams has been really narrow and the competition has been really tight between them.

"I think that's going to be remembered well, and it will be considered as an important step for the Formula E progress, especially on the evolution of the car.

"Season 9 to season 12 [the Gen3 period from 2023-26] is pretty significant on how the technology has evolved towards efficiency."

The arrival of all-wheel drive with the Gen3 Evo car for 2024/25 went a long way to fixing the lack of overtaking in the high-power mode. And with the PitBoost energy top-up stops finally coming in for that same campaign, there was extra flexibility for the FIA with the sporting format - which it diluted somewhat for 2026 as it was clear to competitors, consumers and fans that the races were just too busy and chaotic.

It is also important to remember that traction control limitations were lifted when all-wheel drive came into being in 2025, as they will be for Gen4. Deploying all the power into the wheels with no tyre slip changed the way drivers were conducting their races. This resulted in drivers such as Rowland, Wehrlein and Nick Cassidy really coming to the fore because they saw specific areas in which they could be tactically positive on gaining track position at crucial times.

The Gen3 Evo period also came with an improvement of performance from the Hankook tyres. So too upgrades to the power units themselves.

"The fundamental part was the four-wheel drive mode, but I think it was a package of improvements too," says Martino.

"Because the pure laptimes did already improve as well. It was not only on attack mode during the qualifying session. The overall race performance has improved."

Gen3 certainly created challenges for the teams, but they were mostly overcome.

Will it be remembered fondly? Perhaps by the fans, yes. But by the drivers? Largely not. Many actively disliked Gen3 but that was probably born from the early, troublesome days more than anything.

"We have a much more robust structure today than the one we had in Season 9 [2023] and that is good for all future development of Formula E," adds Martino.

In that sense, and in the circumstances of Gen3's birth, Martino is probably right. Gen3 feels already like a stepping stone to something really special with the potent Gen4 cars.

All kids go through awkward stages growing up. Gen3 was Formula E's later teenage years when it was still discovering itself, still making occasional embarrassing mistakes at the school disco. Now it's time to properly grow up.

"I think we have grown together as a championship," concludes Martino.

"We have built on all this knowledge. Sometimes knowledge comes because of the challenges or things that were not predicted at the very beginning.

"But overall, I think it has been a really positive four years for the championship, and no one can deny that because it has seen a huge evolution in fan base and interaction with the fans."

items.title: Nobody wins from trying to divide F1's fanbase
items.author: Glenn Freeman
items.content:
"There are diehard motorsport fans who talk about clipping during a Formula 1 weekend, but there will also be many who think of a clip as something you put in your hair."

Domenicali has had to fight back against a lot of criticism this year and, as you'd expect from someone in charge of a global institution that is flying high but also under huge pressure to succeed, he'll defend F1 with all he's got. As he should.

But I think it's a risk to regularly paint the "diehard fans" as a minority group who are too negative, prompting Domenicali's recent quotes given to media that featured the suggestion that "negativity gets us nowhere".

I'd agree that after a while, endlessly moaning about F1's engine rules gets a bit old and we all have to live with it. Although, let's not forget, the controversial not-quite-50/50 power split between electrical power and the internal combustion engine is changing for next year to help solve the issues fans and drivers are unhappy with.

However, when things are going well - and in F1's case, they are on several levels at the moment - don't forget the people who got you to the dance. Don't forget that those "diehard fans" are people who stuck by F1 through thick and thin, and were the backbone of a fanbase that was big enough to make Liberty Media think F1 was worth buying in the first place in 2016.

If the F1 bubble pops one day, or even just deflates a bit, it will need those diehards to stick around. If you alienate them while all the charts are pointing 'up and to the right', you run the risk of not having them as a safety net in future.

Glenn spoke about this topic passionately on the latest episode of - you can listen here, or search for it on your podcast platform of choice

None of this is meant to denigrate the vast wave of newer fans F1 has attracted in recent years. I think it would be unfair to suggest that anyone who has discovered F1 in the Liberty/Drive to Survive era is automatically a lightweight fan who isn't interested in anything beyond the surface level. No matter what George Lucas says.

F1's growth should be great for everyone involved, both on the inside and the outside. As someone who remembers being one of only two F1 fans in my entire secondary school at the turn of the century, it's amazing to be on the school run with my own kids today and see how many F1 caps and backpacks there are around. This sport we live and breathe is truly mainstream now and appealing to the next generation, and I love that.

That's why I'm uncomfortable with the notion that new fans and old fans, or new fans and "diehard fans", are two groups that can be divided into ones who are interested in technical details and bring negativity about the current cars, and ones who just want to see action on track.

As someone once told me, 'people don't remain new fans forever'. Eventually many of the ones who stick around want to immerse themselves in what's going on and understand more about it. That doesn't mean they'll all want to know about super clipping one day - I've been an F1 fan since the late-1980s and I'd quite happily never hear about it again!

I wince whenever I see older fans trying to 'gatekeep' F1, but I also don't think it's helpful to declare that people who want to know all the finer details of what's really going on with these highly complex cars are "a niche", as Domenicali recently suggested.

Also, if "the vast majority of people" just want to see action on track, why not do more to make that happen? F1 is expected to have more sprint races in 2027, and as our social media team cheekily noted at Zandvoort, that weekend's sprint was so dull it 'could have been an email'.

If the main focus is for the on-track action to get people out of their seats cheering lots of overtakes, why is F1 so cautious with its sprint format? Why is it just a stint of a grand prix that runs a day early?

I'm all for protecting the sanctity of the grand prix itself. But let's mix the sprints up. Use one shot qualifying to differentiate from the main event and increase the chances of cars qualifying out of position. Or, dare I say it, reverse the grids, even if it's just the top 10.

Arguing over super clips, super chips and hair clips is playground stuff. Let's find something proper to argue about, and see if we can create even more of that all-important action on track while we're at it.

items.title: Winners and losers from MotoGP's Aragon sprint
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Marc Marquez has lived up to his status as pre-weekend favourite at Aragon in the sprint, clawing back some much-needed points in the MotoGP title race.

With no prizes for guessing which category we're placing him in, here are our winners and losers from MotoGP's Saturday action.

Winners: The Marquez brothers (1st and 2nd)

A callback to 2025 not just in it being a Marc-Alex 1-2 - but in the fact it looked fairly uncomplicated.

Once Marc ushered the soft-shod polesitter Marco Bezzecchi to the outside of Turn 1, he was all but assured a straightforward race. 

His title bid needs 37 points here - and it looks like he will get them. He has already all but promised to repeat the same Turn 1 move on Sunday.

On Alex's side, another morsel of evidence that he is a genuine Aragon master - but also a continuation of an increasingly strong season that's not really reflected by the standings.

Loser: Raul Fernandez (8th)

Fernandez doesn't owe anything to Jorge Martin's title bid, but it's probably less than ideal that his race was only notable for roughing up Martin on lap one - before settling into a relatively anonymous ride to eighth.

Once a dominant Moto2 winner at Aragon, Fernandez says he hasn't felt comfortable at the track since its resurfacing, and here unlike his fellow Aprilias he didn't fancy the lifespan of the soft rear.

Eighth is no disaster but being beaten by a KTM and a Honda is underwhelming.

Winner: LCR Honda (7th and 9th)

Team-mate battles are usually zero-sum games but both Diogo Moreira and Johann Zarco are clearly boosting their value this weekend - and both LCR and Honda, which has both riders under contract beyond 2026, have every reason to be delighted.

Zarco really doesn’t look like he’s been out for three months (or even two months, or one month). He led the line for Honda in qualifying and was mixing it in the usual places in the sprint (though he felt a tiny bit of regret in not attacking Fernandez earlier to make his race even better).

And Moreira is clearly exceptionally comfortable this weekend, as evidenced not just by his sprint performance but by the fact he decided not to follow other riders in Q1 and advanced by flying solo.

Loser: Pecco Bagnaia (11th)

This was in some ways what we used to expect from Bagnaia in a sprint - in that he only built into the race once it was already all but over. Except it was transposed much further down the grid than we used to see him.

The end result, thus, is a finish comfortably outside of the points - and the evaluation is much the same as on Friday - a lack of rear grip.

After a mid-season flourish he is firmly in the doldrums again.

Winner: Jack Miller (10th)

The best Yamaha in three of the five comparable sessions so far this weekend, Miller has probably profited at least a little bit from Fabio Quartararo's engine issue (which he'd felt all weekend before it finally gave up the ghost on Saturday).

But even accounting for that, Miller’s probably the faster Yamaha rider right now - suddenly soaring in what we now know for sure to be his last half-season in MotoGP.

Picking off Zarco at the end would've been the cherry on top here, but even without a point a top-10 looks very nice on paper.

Loser: Factory Honda (16th and DNF)

LCR’s rookie and returnee have relegated Honda's actual factory team duo firmly to the status of afterthought so far this weekend.

For what’s supposed to be Honda’s main team, this sprint was effectively over midway through lap one, when Luca Marini slid out of the race - as unlucky collateral in a Miller-Morbidelli-Bastianini incident right ahead of him - three corners after Joan Mir had to pick up his bike and go to last place due to contact through Turn 3 with, again, Enea Bastianini.

But even before that it was unlikely to be a particularly productive race for either Mir or Marini, who aren't dreadfully outmatched but aren't on the level of the LCR duo.

Winner: Pedro Acosta (4th)

Acosta managed to fit in a whole slapstick routine in the moments before lights out, though it was hard to see on the broadcast. Seemingly distracted by Alex Marquez right in front of him, he blew past his grid slot, had to hop off his KTM and reverse, then kicked off a seat winglet as he rushed to hop back on.

The result was a less-than-compliant bike through the fast right-handers and thus a disappointed Acosta, but you really wouldn't know something was amiss if you compared him to his fellow KTM riders, who he ran rings around again.

It seems far-fetched to suggest he could've got much more out of this one.

Loser: Fabio Di Giannantonio (DNF)

Di Giannantonio isn't really winning races this season so his title bid demands extremely dependable points-scoring, with no room for errors - which, however, are increasingly creeping in.

This crash from eighth is much less of a problem than the DNF from the grand prix in Germany, as the points blow today is negligible, and within the Ducati camp he clearly does not have an answer to the Marquez brothers at Aragon.

But the potential confidence blow isn't well-timed.

Winner: Fermin Aldeguer (6th)

Aldeguer needed to qualify better and probably needed a better first lap - but his pace looks pretty electric this weekend, and he had impressively little trouble working his way through the likes of Bagnaia, Zarco, Fernandez and Moreira.

Given his recent injury and given his status as a GP25 rider, this race is another positive signal.

items.title: Marquez regains MotoGP title ground with Aragon sprint win
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Defending MotoGP champion Marc Marquez dominated the Aragon sprint after overtaking title rival Marco Bezzecchi.

Bezzecchi looked to have got a decent enough launch from pole, but Marquez had enough room on the inside to force Bezzecchi to the outside on corner exit - taking the lead and allowing brother Alex Marquez to sneak through, too.

They controlled the race from there, aided by the longer-lasting medium rear tyre, with Bezzecchi never really threatening on the soft rear and ultimately settling into third place.

His team-mate, championship leader Jorge Martin, also ran the soft rear but was frustrated in the early going by fellow Aprilia rider Raul Fernandez - which began as Fernandez retook fourth place on the outside of Turn 2 after losing the spot to Martin at the start.

Their robust wheel-to-wheel racing later into the lap dropped both behind KTM's Pedro Acosta, before Martin cleared Fernandez and went back past Acosta.

But the medium rear-shod Acosta bided his time behind the points leader and when Martin made a mistake at the penultimate corner, Acosta went past and consolidated fourth.

Martin's fifth-place finish means he is now 29 points ahead of Bezzecchi and 33 ahead of race winner Marquez. The injury-absent Ai Ogura is 42 back and Fabio Di Giannantonio remains 46 adrift, after crashing out from eighth place early on.

Fermin Aldeguer was 10th after the start but scythed his way through into sixth place by the end of the race, overtaking Diogo Moreira on the final lap - with Moreira settling for top Honda honours in seventh.

Fernandez and Johann Zarco, Aldeguer's fellow injury returnee and Moreira's LCR team-mate, completed the points-scoring top nine, with Jack Miller just a tenth away from picking up a point from Yamaha.

The only other rider to crash besides Di Giannantonio was Luca Marini, who exited the race on the opening lap.

Fabio Quartararo also didn't finish, his Yamaha suffering what looked like an engine blow-up just before halfway.

items.title: Bezzecchi upsets Marquez for Aragon MotoGP pole
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Marco Bezzecchi upset pre-weekend favourite Marc Marquez to claim MotoGP pole position for the Aragon Grand Prix.

Bezzecchi was the only rider setting sub-1m45s laps, so saw off Marquez by 0.089s - the latter threatening the benchmark in the final seconds but messing up the entry to Turn 14 and having to settle for second.

Alex Marquez will join the pair on the front row for the sprint and for Sunday's main event.

Raul Fernandez, points leader Jorge Martin and Pedro Acosta will complete row two. Acosta set his best lap in the elder Marquez's tow, before sliding off on entry into Reverse Corkscrew while trying to improve.

VR46 team-mates Fabio Di Giannantonio and Franco Morbidelli ran together on track and were split by just three tenths in the end, but that also meant five positions, Di Giannantonio in seventh and Morbidelli in 12th.

Between them were Pecco Bagnaia, Johann Zarco, Diogo Moreira and Fermin Aldeguer. Bagnaia and Moreira had advanced from Q1, despite Moreira crashing late in that session.

Jack Miller, whose impending departure from Pramac Yamaha (and MotoGP as a whole) was announced earlier this week, placed 13th as the best of the Yamahas and the best-of-the-rest in Q1 - ahead of good friend and future World Superbike rival Brad Binder (KTM).

Joan Mir had a last-second shot at picking off Moreira for the final Q2 spot but came up two tenths short and settled for 15th - though did outqualify team-mate Luca Marini for the 12th time in 13 attempts this season.

items.title: Our verdict on Norris's deal + state of the F1 driver market
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
The long-term Formula 1 driver deals keep coming, as defending champion Lando Norris has extended his stay at McLaren until at least 2030.

That's in line with the recent announcement that four-time F1 champion Max Verstappen will remain at Red Bull until the same year, while Charles Leclerc's contract at Ferrari could run even longer than that.

Norris's stock right now is arguably the highest it's ever been; as defending champion, he has also won the two most recent races as McLaren's 2026 development begins to bear fruit.

So was a berth anywhere else realistic? What does this say about the driver market? And what are the consequences of more and more longer-term deals being announced?

Here are our team's thoughts:

The F1 driver market is dead

It's unfortunate how static the F1 driver market is at the sharp end.

This is not a point about Norris or McLaren specifically - this is a sage deal for both parties - but it feels like whatever incentive structure existed in the past for drivers to sign shorter-term or properly explore alternative options and try to manoeuvre themselves is totally, totally gone.

It may have been gone already for a decade or so, but it feels like something you could connect to the explosion in team valuations under Liberty Media. A driver salary cap to go with the cost cap was explored but never introduced and while that's good from a labour point of view, it means truly generational wealth is available to all the top drivers rather than just outliers such as Michael Schumacher and Lewis Hamilton in the past.

These deals create security against the natural ebb and flow of a driver's market value. And changing teams is hard, so is a great way of accidentally tanking that market value. It's different in other sports - when you go from, say, Tottenham to Bayern in football, you don't need to learn an all-new ball, you just need to adjust to actually winning games for a change.

And, yes, Hamilton-to-Ferrari was an exception but if he were 15 years younger, he'd obviously be on a Mercedes deal to 2035 right now.

No possible reason to look elsewhere

While Verstappen and Red Bull is defining team/driver partnership of the 2020s, Norris and McLaren isn't so far behind. Therefore, it's logical for this alliance to keep a long timeline in place.

The choice of 2030 aligns well with F1's rules cycles and also other deals, such as Verstappen's recently announced Red Bull contract. There are similarities there in that Norris has had enormous success with McLaren and clearly feels very comfortable there, but the difference is that, right now, McLaren has less to prove to Norris than Red Bull has to Verstappen.

Therefore, there's no possible reason for Norris to look elsewhere, while from McLaren's perspective it is wise to lock down Norris and continues to hold flexibility on Oscar Piastri's seat.

That said, Piastri's contract still has plenty of time on it, so there's not necessarily need for urgency in extending that, which gives McLaren the flexibility should it want to make a move for someone else down the line. But don't underestimate how strong a two-driver line-up this is.

A big downside to these big contracts

For McLaren and Norris this is the best thing to do: given the opportunity (car) he is winning races and McLaren has the determination under Zak Brown's leadership to get back to its heydays of being a consistent championship-winning team.

Also to add to that, in reality, where else is there to go that would give a winning car and a team relationship that Norris currently has?

Piastri has had his chance to show what he is worth and he is very good, so I wouldn't be surprised to see him also continue with McLaren. Why not? He fits in well and, again, when he has the opportunity (car) he can win races.

However, these long-term contracts are closing the doors to potential up-and-coming drivers and with more or less no testing available to show a driver's talent, how is anyone going to show their worth? Take Leonardo Fornaroli, McLaren reserve and the reigning Formula 2 champion, for example: what happens to him?

F1 keeps talking about finding true talent, it even talks about getting a female into F1, but can someone please explain to me how these scenarios can happen? Yes, we have testing of previous cars opportunities, but who really pays any attention to that?

Something needs to be done as the stepping stones to F1 through Formula 3 and F2 are just too expensive. It's always been the same and as Alpine has proven with re-signing Franco Colapinto, money is much more important than talent.

Norris's extension puts Piastri in an interesting spot.

I have zero doubt McLaren doesn't mind which of its drivers is winning races or championships, but only one of them has been doing that recently.

So you can imagine how McLaren is starting to become Norris's team. Not that it's favouring him but it's naturally going to start coalescing around the stronger driver, in terms of direction.

Therefore you could see why Piastri (and manager Mark Webber) might be considering whether his long-term future should be at McLaren, beyond his likely-end-of-2028 deal.

The problem is his stock's taken a knock versus 12 months ago. Since then, he's blown a decent title lead and has looked firmly second-best to Norris this year with too many weekends, by his own admission, spent too far off the pace.

So while it's tempting to wonder whether Piastri could be a project leader for someone such as Audi or Aston Martin - and I think he has the raw ability to be - he's got to first get himself out of this current hole or risk being an unattractive second-best to Norris.

The market is a very different beast these days

With what has all the makings of a great Shakespearean play, the House of McLaren, the House of Ferrari and the House of Red Bull are now locked in following Norris's contract extension until 2030.

Where once F1's driver market was a source of intrigue and excitement, machinations on this front have now stopped.

Instead, loyalty, stability and family are the order of the day. Verstappen and Leclerc have now been joined by Norris in taking themselves off the market for a while; and expect Mercedes to shore up its own situation pretty soon.

Stability may be less exciting than the drama of a big silly-season switch but it's the logical outcome in an era of F1 where the cost cap appears (thanks to legacy infrastructure reasons) to have helped edge the top four clear of the pack for now - so prime seats are increasingly rare.

The pool of favourable options is narrowed down even more once one team locks in one of their A* drivers, as that makes becoming their team-mate less exciting because it means going up against another big gun with the same equipment.

Better to be the big fish in your own still very big pond and make it the best one of there, than face the headaches that come from a topline driver rivalry.

Leclerc, Verstappen and Norris all settling down makes perfect sense.

Is it exciting for gossip? No. But the family dynasties are now in play to shape F1 until the end of this ruleset, and that in itself is going to throw up plenty of its own drama.

McLaren has earned Norris's trust

Of all the top teams in recent years, McLaren has proven it is better at developing a car than the rest - so if you're Norris, McLaren is the only option.

Sure, Mercedes has started this cycle with a better package, but that was inevitable as soon as it was confirmed McLaren would remain a Mercedes customer for this ruleset.

McLaren is fighting Mercedes with one arm tied behind its back given it gets data last-minute from weekend to weekend and doesn't have access to the data Mercedes has had while building this power unit. McLaren has no right being as close as it is. The last two tracks may have flattered it but it's clear McLaren is developing towards Mercedes again and is trending in the right direction.

The only real downside is that power unit deficit as a customer, but as the rules cycle wears on that will be less of an issue as the status quo sets in. And in those circumstances, in the last ruleset McLaren became F1's top squad.

With Leclerc and Verstappen tied down at the other top teams, and Kimi Antonelli set to lead Mercedes for as long as he wants to be there, there's no better option for Norris. And even if one of those other teams had an opening, McLaren has earned Norris's trust. It wasted a bit of his early career with poor cars but is certainly making up for that now.

Going elsewhere is going to get harder

On one level I get this: stability, trust, faith, reward etc.

On the other, you could look at it as somewhat shut off and lacking ambition for fresher challenges that can come up. Even, perhaps, dare one say that Norris may have a bit of Stockholm Syndrome in F1.

He's only ever known Zak Brown-era McLaren. Of course, it's served him well with a title and 13 grand prix wins so far. But by 2030 he will have raced for the same team for 12 seasons and if he needs or wants a change how much of a shock to the system will that be for him? And would he be able to adapt?

You presume that for a driver of Norris's class it would be straightforward. But the longer he stays with a single team the harder it will get as more Antonellis come on to the scene.

The bigger question also here I feel is how Norris can stay hungry, motivated and avoid future burnout.

Contesting 25 grands prix a year (as will surely soon become the norm) over a decade-long-plus stretch is a big ask for anyone. Mika Hakkinen had to stop after a similar period, and so did Fernando Alonso to an extent with his World Endurance Championship and Indycar 'break' - and in both of those cases that was with much fewer grands prix on the calendar.

Perhaps modern drivers are more conditioned for the constant grind and can soak it up better through more understanding of the mental stress these days, which is of course a good thing and one that Norris can keep on top of.

items.title: Norris extends McLaren F1 contract with bumper new deal
items.author: Jack Benyon
items.content:
Reigning Formula 1 world champion Lando Norris has extended his McLaren contract, taking his stay with the team beyond a decade and through the 2030 season.

But there is scope for that to run longer - as McLaren's announcement of the deal added there was a "multi-year option to commit beyond" that 2030 date.

Norris, who has won the last two F1 races in the upgraded McLaren, became part of McLaren's junior programme in 2017 and earned a race drive for 2019.

He has already notched the highest number of starts of any McLaren driver and is on course to extend that record substantially with his new deal.

It means Norris joins rivals Charles Leclerc and Max Verstappen in being signed at least through the 2030 season, the planned end of the current engine rules cycle unless an earlier switch to V8s is agreed for 2030.

"McLaren is my home, and I'm very pleased to be signing a new contract to keep me with the team until at least 2030," said Norris.

"When I started this journey nine years ago, I was clear about the goals I wanted to achieve: to get McLaren back to the front and to win championships. We've achieved that goal, but we want more, we want to keep on winning, and we know as a team that we're capable of achieving it."

Team principal Andrea Stella said Norris had been an "integral" part of McLaren's success, and was a "special human" and "exceptional driver".

McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown added: "His journey with the team is a fantastic example of our commitment to identifying, developing and supporting world-class talent, and his achievements speak for themselves."

As part of the deal, Norris will be gifted an MCL39 car from his 2025 title-winning year, a "lasting reminder of his contribution to the team".

Norris's deal was the soonest to expire of the lead figures at McLaren, with team-mate Oscar Piastri having committed to the end of 2028 last year, while Brown and Stella agreed new deals within the last two years.

items.title: When does each 2026 F1 driver's contract expire?
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
Save for the significant arrival of a new Formula 1 team and two returning drivers, there were scarcely any changes to the grid for 2026.

But that could all change over the remainder of the season, as more than 50% of the field are due to be out of contract come the end of the year.

Here's what you need to know about when each driver's contract ends.

Lando Norris - 2030Oscar Piastri - 2028

McLaren announced Norris had committed to a new deal through to 2030 - with the option for longer - in late-August, at a point where the defending F1 champion had also won the two most recent grands prix.

Piastri extended his contract in March 2025 with a "multi-year" deal that you'd suspect will keep him at McLaren until the end of 2028 at least.

George Russell - 2027Kimi Antonelli - 2026

F1 2026's two title protagonists were only officially confirmed for this season in October last year.

Russell's contract is understood to run into 2027, though the way it was presented could still leave both team and driver free to do something different next year.

Max Verstappen - 2030Isack Hadjar - 2026

After months (well, years) of speculation about Verstappen's future at the team, Red Bull made the surprise announcement ahead of the 2026 Dutch GP that the four-time F1 champion had agreed a new deal that is due to keep him there until 2030.

Hadjar was brought into the Red Bull line-up at the expense of Yuki Tsunoda - that announcement stated only that he would be part of the 2026 line-up - and has compared reasonably well to Verstappen in his first season in the senior team, even if the car's overall competitiveness has been a limiting factor.

Charles Leclerc - 2030+Lewis Hamilton - 2027

In announcing Charles Leclerc's deal had been renewed, Ferrari released an ambiguous statement ahead of the Monaco Grand Prix that was light on details and stated merely that he would "continue to wear the team's colours for the coming seasons".

As Leclerc's existing arrangement (also publicly announced at the time only as being for "several more seasons") was in place until 2029, The Race understands that the new deal is an extension to that and as such will keep him at Ferrari until beyond 2030 - the current longest F1 driver contract.

While the length of Lewis Hamilton's contract has never been made official, it was widely accepted to be a two-year-minimum affair and the seven-time champion said at the recent Canadian GP that he was committed at least until the end of 2027.

Alex Albon - 2027Carlos Sainz - 2028

Williams used the week leading up to the Dutch GP to separately announce that both drivers would be staying on beyond the end of the 2026 season.

In the case of Albon, his deal was presented as an "extension" for 2027 - although his existing contract was thought to cover next year already. The Race understands no new racing contract had been agreed and, instead, that the 2027 confirmation relates to exit clauses that existed in the contract.

Sainz, meanwhile, agreed a multi-year contract extension that did not specify the length of his contract but will include options over forthcoming years.

Liam Lawson - 2026Arvid Lindblad - 2026

Lawson regrouped well following his demotion to Racing Bulls just two rounds into the 2025 season, sufficiently so that he was retained for 2026.

Lindblad, the only rookie in this year's field, scored points on an eye-catching debut at the Australian GP and added to his tally in the Canadian GP sprint race.

They have been presented as Racing Bulls's drivers for 2026 only.

Fernando Alonso - 2026Lance Stroll - 2026

Two-time champion Alonso and Stroll are currently contracted only until the end of a gruelling first year (that is at least on an upward trajectory) of Aston Martin's works partnership with Honda.

Ollie Bearman - 2026Esteban Ocon - 2026

Though both Bearman and Ocon are contracted until the end of the current season, Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu recently had to shut down "bulls***" speculation of a rift between Ocon and himself, and the possibility of a mid-season split.

Nico Hulkenberg - "multi-year"Gabriel Bortoleto - "multi-year"

Audi's having a mixed first season in F1 - with a decent turn of speed being paired with more reliability issues than it would like - and should really have more points on the board than the two Bortoleto scored at the season opener.

The 21-year-old is racing alongside Hulkenberg for a second season, following the team's transition from Sauber into the works team.

Hulkenberg's deal includes 2025 and 2026, though reports have suggested 2027 is in the mix as well.

Pierre Gasly - 2028Franco Colapinto - 2027

Alpine executive advisor Flavio Briatore initially held out on committing to Colapinto - keeping his options open in case Verstappen moved to Mercedes and one of Russell or Antonelli became available - but the 23-year-old has since been retained for 2027, which will be his second full campaign in F1.

Sergio Perez - 2027Valtteri Bottas - 2027

Grand prix veterans Perez and Bottas were both signed on "multi-year" deals that brought them back to the grid with the new Cadillac team.

Perez has generally been the more impressive of the two so far in 2026, though speculation that Bottas's place could be at risk - for now or for 2027 - appears to be wide of the mark.
